files.about: Every game in the Child I Fun project is built from the files in this library. Each file does one job, starts with a short header that says what it does, and can be reused in any new game.

Colors, faces, and animations for every character: the robot (worried, brave, happy, surprised, thinking faces; chest spark that grows with courage), Sunny, Rigel, Professor Kepler, flames, and the hop, walk, tremble, blink, and wag motions.
Professor Kepler, the mossy rock with tiny round glasses. Sits at (0, 0), about 52 units tall.

Nova, a teeny baby Spinosaurus with a coral sail, a long snout, and a glowing star lantern. Her outline is one solid dinosaur shape (tail, spiny sail, snout, legs, and claws), plus a jaw that can open. Filled solid black and made huge, that same outline is the giant shadow everyone calls Shadowspine, toothy grin and all.
files.provides: Kit.art.nova { SHAPES, HINGE, COLORS, g(options), shadow(fill, jawDegrees), svg(options, size), url(options, size), path2d() }
files.notes:
options = { face: smile | happy | worried | surprised, lantern: true (default) | false, flip: true to face left }
Drawing space: facing right, feet at y = 0, about 62 units tall (x from -60 to 52, y from -62 to 1).
SHAPES: body (one outline: tail, body, sail, neck, head and upper teeth, both legs), jaw (lower jaw with teeth), arm.
HINGE is where the jaw turns. shadow() draws the three shapes in one color (the jaw a little open for a grin), and path2d()
gives the same shapes for canvas drawing, so a game can make the shadow laugh by turning the jaw around HINGE.

files.about: Rigel the penguin in a bubble helmet and a pink scarf. Stands at (0, 0), about 48 units tall.
Small round head portraits of the robot, Sunny, Rigel, and Professor Kepler, used in the friends bar and on helper buttons.
files.provides: Kit.art.portraits { robot, dog, peng, rock } (SVG markup strings, viewBox -16 -16 32 32)

files.about: Sunny, the fluffy magic puppy (black, white, and tan curls, floppy ears, star collar, sparkles, wagging tail). Built in code so the curls stay even. Sits at (0, 0), about 66 units tall.
files.provides: Kit.art.puppy() -> SVG markup string

files.about: The tall robot hero, side view, standing at (0, 0) and about 200 units tall. Contains every face (worried, brave, happy, surprised, thinking); characters.css picks which one shows from the robot's class and data-face. Place inside <g class="robot" id="robot">.
The robot drawn small on a canvas for walkable maps: legs swing and arms pump while walking, eyes look the way he's heading, and his chest glows brighter with courage.
files.provides: Kit.art.drawRobotTop(ctx, x, y, t, motion, { tokens, glow })
files.notes:
motion = { moving, phase, fx, fy } from kit/topdown-map.js; glow = 0 to 1 chest brightness.
tokens needs: metal, metalShade, copper, glass, snow, void, cRobot

files.about: T-Rexy, a cute cartoony green T-Rex with a big head, a big eye, two tiny teeth, and famously tiny arms. Also draws his family (same shape, different colors and accessories). Poses for standing, running, hopping, and sitting. Big shiny eyes and a little brow that shows his mood, with faces for happy, excited (star-sparkle eyes), determined, blinking, worried (with a sweat drop), surprised, thinking, dizzy, and sleepy. Plus unlockable looks: hats (space helmet, wizard hat, DJ headphones, glitch crown, party hat, star shades), things on his back (rocket backpack, super cape), and colors (galaxy purple, golden, ocean blue, bubblegum pink).
files.provides: Kit.art.trexy { COLORS, LOOKS, g(options), svg(options, size), url(options, size), isTall(options) }
files.notes:
options = { pose: stand | run1 | run2 | hop | sit,
            face: smile | happy | excited | determined | blink | worried | surprised | think | dizzy | sleepy,
            who: trexy | mom | dad | sis (colors), acc: none | flower | glasses | bow | cap | a hat from LOOKS.head,
            back: none | a back item from LOOKS.back, skin: a color from LOOKS.skin (overrides who), flip: true to face left }
Drawing space: facing right, feet at y = 0, about 100 units tall (x from -58 to 54, y from -94 to 2).
Tall hats reach up to y = -124: for those, isTall(options) is true and svg() makes the picture 130 units tall instead of 100
(same width, extra room on top), so draw it 1.3 times taller to keep T-Rexy the same size.
svg() returns a standalone <svg> (for images and canvas drawing); url() returns it as a data URL.
LOOKS = { head: { id: name }, back: { id: name }, skin: { id: name } }, the names shown to players.

files.about: Shared shapes referenced with <use>: the flame (flamePath, base at 0,0, 40 units tall) and the four-point twinkle star (spark4). Place inside an inline SVG's <defs>.
Simple filled icons used on buttons so the game needs fewer words: back, go, retry, rocket, check, eye, music note, play, stop, and a shovel.
files.provides: Kit.art.icons { back, go, retry, rocket, check, eye, note, play, stop, shovel } (SVG markup strings)

files.about: Art for the top-down map of Lumina: dusty ground with craters, rocks, and glowing mushrooms, dotted paths, Comet Crater, the Old Observatory, Glowworm Grove, the Sleepy Village, the launch pad, gold star beacons with progress dots, and the glowing launch ring.
files.provides: Kit.art.luminaMap { makeDecor, drawGround, drawPaths, drawCrater, drawObservatory, drawGrove, drawVillage, drawPad, drawBeacon, drawPadRing }
files.notes:
Every draw function takes the canvas context first and a tokens object T (colors read from CSS) last.
T needs: void, gold, good, cPeng, stoneSh, metalShade, wall, roof, win, leaf, trunk, dome, scope

files.about: Four detailed memory pictures for jigsaw puzzles, drawn in SVG: home in Fern Valley at night, the family dinner, the bedroom at 11:11, and the swirly galaxy swoop. Each one hides a clue for the mystery if you look closely. Also draws the spiral galaxies used everywhere in the game.
files.provides: Kit.art.memories { home, dinner, window, swoop } (each a function returning a standalone 400 x 300 <svg>), galaxy(cx, cy, r, turn, colors, arms), note(x, y, scale, color), CLUE_SPOTS, clueTiles(name, rows, cols)
files.notes:
Clues hidden in the pictures: a tiny glowing music box on the hill (home), salad AND meat on the table plus a little teal tail sneaking
out the door past the basket of fish (dinner), tiny three-toed footprints on the windowsill and a huge moth-shaped shadow made by a teeny
moth near the lamp (window), and someone small on a floating rock holding a star lantern (swoop).
Lots of little extras to spot, too: a rocket weathervane, a T-REXY mailbox, a volcano, The Big Book of Volcanoes, a BLAST OFF poster,
fireflies, and T-Rexy's cap flying off in the swoop.

files.about: "Corona Blaze": a fast, driving adventure tune for the fiery nebula and the tower climb. 128 bpm, A minor. Song format is described in kit/music.js.
files.provides: Kit.songs.corona

files.about: "Echo Rings": the first portal: bright and bouncy with a big echo on the lead, and its chorus hides the first piece of the weird music. 140 bpm, A major. Song format is described in kit/groove.js.
files.provides: Kit.songs.echo

files.about: "Fern Moon Feast": the second portal: a hoppy, oom-pah dinner dance with the second piece of the weird music. 144 bpm, G major. Song format is described in kit/groove.js.
files.provides: Kit.songs.fern

files.about: "Glacia Twinkle": a high, icy, plucked tune for the frozen planet. 92 bpm, E major. Song format is described in kit/music.js.
files.provides: Kit.songs.glacia

files.about: "Glitch Hub Bounce": the bouncy theme for the title screen and the crash pad: a happy, head-bobbing groove with claps and sparkly arpeggios. 128 bpm, F major. Song format is described in kit/groove.js.
files.provides: Kit.songs.glitchHub

files.about: "Home Stomp": the ending: the lullaby turned into a huge, happy dance party. 160 bpm, C major. Song format is described in kit/groove.js.
files.provides: Kit.songs.homeStomp

files.about: "Lantern Lab": the third portal: glowing and sparkly, full of twinkling arpeggios, with the third piece of the weird music. 148 bpm, D major. Song format is described in kit/groove.js.
files.provides: Kit.songs.lantern

files.about: "Lumina in the Dark": a slow, soft music-box tune for the sleeping home world. 74 bpm, A minor. Song format is described in kit/music.js.
files.provides: Kit.songs.lumina

files.about: "Meridian Stargazer": a thoughtful, wandering tune for the stony planet of the old stargazer. 88 bpm, G minor. Song format is described in kit/music.js.
files.provides: Kit.songs.meridian

files.about: "Nimbus Bounce": a bouncy square-wave tune for the cotton-candy cloud planet. 120 bpm, D major. Song format is described in kit/music.js.
files.provides: Kit.songs.nimbus

files.about: "Nova's Lullaby": the weird music itself: a high, squeaky music-box lullaby, with a soft tick-tock beat and twinkles. 112 bpm, C major. Song format is described in kit/groove.js.
files.provides: Kit.songs.lullaby

files.about: "Lumina Reborn": the happy ending tune when the Everlight comes home. 108 bpm, C major. Song format is described in kit/music.js.
files.provides: Kit.songs.reborn

files.about: "Shadow Run": the chase through the Shadow Gate: sneaky and silly-spooky in a minor key, but still a bouncy dance. 156 bpm, D minor. Song format is described in kit/groove.js.
files.provides: Kit.songs.shadowRun

files.about: "Starward Theme": the cheerful main tune for the title screen and flights. 104 bpm, C major. Song format is described in kit/music.js.
files.provides: Kit.songs.theme

files.about: "Whirlpool Warp": the fourth portal: swirly sixteenth-note runs, and its chorus is the whole weird tune at last. 152 bpm, E major. Song format is described in kit/groove.js.
files.provides: Kit.songs.whirl

files.about: Rocket motion and display: liftoff rise, hover bob, launch rumble, engine flame stretch, plus the rocket previews in the side panel (build progress, part slots, finished ship).
The buildable rocket. Data for every part choice and paint color, plus a drawing function that renders any combination (missing parts can show as dashed outlines, and one part can be highlighted).
files.provides: Kit.art.rocket { PARTS, PART_ORDER, PAINTS, PAINT_ORDER, ENGINE_COLORS, svg(config, options), box(innerSvg, cls), partIcons }

files.about: A side-view spaceship built from four parts, each with its own style choices: cockpit (bubble, dino head, crystal), wings (fern leaf, bat, lightning), thrusters (one, two, three), and a glitch core in a neon color. Five neon paint jobs. Missing parts can show as dashed outlines, a pilot can peek out of the cockpit, and the ship can wake up with a face on its nose.
files.provides: Kit.art.ship { PARTS, PART_ORDER, PAINTS, PAINT_ORDER, CORES, svg(config, options), box(inner, cls), url(config, options, size), partIcons }
files.notes:
config  = { cockpit, wings, thrusters, core, paint } (any can be missing)
options = { ghost: draw missing parts dashed, hl: part key to highlight, flame: engine flames, pilot: markup for a head in the cockpit,
            face: awake | blink | happy (eyes and a smile on the nose, for a ship that has come alive) }
Drawing space: facing right, centered on 0,0, viewBox -64 -42 128 84.

files.about: Six real recorded cute creature noises for the dinosaurs: happy chirps, coos, a hum, a "wheee!", an excited "ooh!", and a curious "hm?". They come from the "80 CC0 creature SFX" pack by rubberduck on OpenGameArt, which is CC0 (public domain: free to use, credit is kind but not required). Each one is trimmed, made about as loud as the others, and squeezed into a small mono MP3 written right into this file, so the game stays one self-contained page.
files.provides: Kit.sounds.dinoChirps: [{ id, mood (happy | excited | curious), seconds, from (the name in the original pack), src (a data: URL of the MP3) }], Kit.sounds.credits
files.notes:
Source: https://opengameart.org/content/80-cc0-creature-sfx (the "cute" sounds), license: https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/zero/1.0/
Kit.voices.chirp plays these, sped up or slowed down so each dinosaur sounds like itself (a bigger dinosaur gets a lower voice).
chirp: a quick, high chirp that slides down. ooh: an "ooOOoo!" that swoops up and back down. hum: a cozy, happy hum.
wee: a "wheee!" that climbs up high. huh: a little "hm?" that goes up at the end. coo: a soft coo that rises and falls.
To swap in a different noise: trim it, make it mono, encode it as a small MP3 (about 64 kbps), and replace a src. Keep seconds accurate.

files.about: Two real recorded cartoon villain laughs for Shadowspine: high, cackly "HA-HA-HA-HAAA!"s. They come from the "Evil Laughs" pack by Eldritch Grim on OpenGameArt, which is CC0 (public domain: free to use, credit is kind but not required). Each one is trimmed, made about as loud as the other, and squeezed into a small mono MP3 written right into this file, so the game stays one self-contained page.
files.provides: Kit.sounds.villainLaughs: [{ id, seconds, from (the name in the original pack), src (a data: URL of the MP3) }], Kit.sounds.credits
files.notes:
Source: https://opengameart.org/content/evil-laughs-pack ("Laugh 4" and "Laugh 7"), license: https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/zero/1.0/
Kit.voices.evilLaugh plays these when they're in the game (taking turns), and falls back to its made-in-code laugh when they aren't.
To swap in a different laugh: trim it, make it mono, encode it as a small MP3 (about 64 kbps), and replace a src. Keep seconds accurate.

files.about: The Corona Nebula scenery: a tall three-floor tower whose windows light up as data-floors goes from 1 to 3, in a 400 by 260 scene. Shows when the scene's data-world is "corona".
Planet Glacia scenery: clusters of ice spikes on both sides of a 400 by 260 scene. Shows when the scene's data-world is "glacia".

Canvas backgrounds for the Glitch Nebula, each world a neon take on a famous NASA space picture: the Cosmic Cliffs of the Carina Nebula (the crash pad), the Southern Ring Nebula (Echo Rings), the Pillars of Creation (Fern Moon), a blazing Wolf-Rayet star in its clumpy shell (Lantern Lab), the Whirlpool Galaxy and its little companion (Whirlpool Galaxy), and the Horsehead Nebula (the Shadow Gate), plus the Milky Way and the Andromeda Galaxy over Fern Valley at night. Every sky also gets glowing gas made from noise, dark dust lanes, stars with Webb-style eight-point spikes, tiny far-away galaxies like a deep field, and a mix of drifting galaxies (spirals, tilted spirals, and edge-on ones like the Sombrero). Gentle glitches nudge a stripe of the sky sideways now and then. Can also draw the giant black Shadowspine on the clouds, with an optional tiny lantern glow at its feet. Each world has its own colors for runs, too.
files.provides: Kit.art.nebula { THEMES, create() -> { draw(ctx, view, options) } }
files.notes:
view = { w, h, T (pixels per tile), camX, camY, t (ms), dpr }
options = { theme, shadow: { x (screen fraction 0 to 1), k (size, 1 = normal), lantern: true | false, jaw (degrees open), shake (0 to 1) } | null, whisper: true (rarely
            shows a tiny hidden message inside a glitch), glitch: false to turn glitches off }
Each theme: sky (top and bottom colors), blobs (three glow colors), scene (how its gas is shaped), land (its big landmark),
plus the colors runs use (edge, block, spike, pad, piece, spark, portals). Skies and landmarks are painted once and reused,
so drawing a frame is just a few pictures. The sky strip repeats seamlessly as the camera moves.
Gentle on purpose: glitches happen at most about once a second, last a tenth of a second, and only shift a thin stripe.
Nothing flashes more than three times a second. With "reduce motion" turned on there are no glitches and nothing spins.
Inspired by NASA, ESA, CSA, and STScI pictures from the Hubble and Webb space telescopes; everything here is drawn by code.

files.about: Ground gradients for side-view worlds. Their colors come from --ground-a and --ground-b, so each world recolors them in worlds.css. Place inside an inline SVG's <defs>.

Lumina seen from the side as a small round planet that turns under the robot. Five places sit around it: launch pad (0 degrees), Comet Crater (72), Old Observatory (144), Glowworm Grove (216), Sleepy Village (288). Rotate #spin to walk between them. Windows and glowworms light up when the world is "luminaLit".
Planet Meridian scenery: carved standing stones and an old brass telescope on a tripod, in a 400 by 260 scene. Shows when the scene's data-world is "meridian".
Planet Nimbus scenery: puffy pink clouds on both sides of a 400 by 260 scene. Shows when the scene's data-world is "nimbus".
A wide curved hill for side-view planets, drawn in a 400 by 260 scene. Colored by the current world.

Colors and scenery rules for every side-view world (Lumina dark and lit, Nimbus, Glacia, Meridian, Corona): sky, ground, planet in the sky, which scenery shows, buildings, ice, stones, the tower windows, and the Everlight flame.
files.notes: Set data-world on the .scene element to switch worlds. Add .flying to drop the ground away during flights.

files.about: Assembles a game (or the library page) from its separate files into one self-contained web page, checks that every file's
files.requires: are loaded first, and writes catalog.json, the list of every file and what it does.
files.notes:
Usage, from the library folder:
  python3 build/build.py games/starward/game.json   build one game into dist/
  python3 build/build.py site/site.json            build the library page (index.html)
  python3 build/build.py --catalog                 rewrite catalog.json from the file headers
  python3 build/build.py --all                     catalog, every buildable game, then the library page

A game.json lists: title, output, fonts, styles (CSS in order), body (HTML with <!-- @include path --> lines),
scripts (shared Kit modules, assets, and content, in load order), and parts (the game's own files, which share one scope).

files.about: Automated play-test for the library: checks file headers, checks the built pages match the source, loads every page in headless Chromium at Chromebook size, and plays Starward and Mini Game Survival start to finish (every run, puzzle, flight, and secret, the ending, and the high score). Must pass before every commit that changes library/.
files.notes:
Usage, from anywhere:
  python3 library/build/playtest.py            everything (about 4 minutes)
  python3 library/build/playtest.py --quick    skip the full playthroughs
  add -v to print every screen, or --shots=DIR to save a screenshot of each Mini Game Survival screen

Needs Python 3 and Playwright. If missing:
  pip install playwright            (add --break-system-packages on Claude's workspace)
  python3 -m playwright install chromium

Checks:
  1. Headers: every source file starts with @file (its own path) and @about.
  2. Build: build.py --all, run on a copy, reproduces dist/, catalog.json, and index.html byte for byte.
  3. Pages: every built game, legacy game, and the library page load at 1366x768 with no page
     errors and no sideways scroll. Built games and the library page also allow no console errors.
     Pages are served inside the same wrapper claude.ai adds when it publishes (its base styles
     hide [hidden] elements, for example), so the test sees what Child I sees. Google Fonts is
     blocked so the run doesn't depend on outside network.
  4. Starward playthrough, with a fresh browser (so adaptive levels start at their defaults):
     - Title: name the robot and start.
     - Lumina map: walk to each place by clicking the map. The first puzzle takes three wrong
       answers; "Show me" must stay hidden until the third, then appear and reveal the answer. The second uses the Scan helper.
       Every dig must show its one-line tip, every dig is typed, every part style picked, then back to the launch pad to paint the ship.
     - Right answers: every puzzle must cheer, show no Next button, and move on by itself within 5 seconds.
     - Tapping friends: the first puzzle with Sunny on the crew is solved after tapping Sunny on the stage (her clue must
       appear), and the first with Rigel after tapping Rigel in the friends bar (a letter must appear).
     - Flights: the first try of the first flight is typed badly on purpose and must offer
       "Fly again"; every other flight is typed cleanly and must land, and the landing screen must move on by itself.
     - All planet puzzles answered, the brave words typed, and the ending reached.
     - High score: a name saves, gets a rank, and shows on the board as a score on this computer.
  5. Mini Game Survival, with fresh browsers:
     - The question library is checked (8 versions of every mystery question, each answer one of its options, Nova never named
       before the reveal; 6 clue lines at each typing level; 8 science facts, 14 bonus facts, and 4 memory texts per portal; no
       repeats; plenty of clue words at each level), and so is the dealer: every version comes up once before any repeats, never
       twice in a row, and a half-used deck carries over to the next game.
     - Memory pieces and beats: 90 runs are built at levels 1 to 6. Every piece must be catchable on the winning and secret
       routes, every chunk must start on the music's beat, and a hop pressed right on the beat must clear the first obstacle
       of every chunk one hop can clear. The recorded villain laughs and dino noises must decode, and the dino noises must
       cover every mood and make sound at every voice pitch.
     - Easy mode: L and R move through story lines; the first run must be level 1 (the slowest) with checkpoints on,
       pressing again in the air must double hop, R must skip the run, and the memory must then have holes (clues kept).
     - The full playthrough is in Hard mode. No screen may show a count of attempts.
     - Title, then the story lines (Enter), then the crash pad: switch modes there and back, type ROAR and poke Shadowspine
       (Easter eggs), take a look off and on in T-Rexy's closet, click each portal.
     - Runs: checkpoints are on from the start (no Checkpoints button). The first run is left alone until T-Rexy crashes
       twice: a crash with no key pressed must show a Hint with the keys, the first crash must send him back to the start,
       and the music must be in time with the run. Then the built-in autopilot (the level's own solution, sped up) finishes
       every run and takes the secret route, so all four hidden diary pages must be found. R must not skip a Hard run.
       Fern Moon misses 3 pieces on purpose and is run again with A; Lantern Lab misses 2 and must offer only Run it again.
       Every run must end with every piece caught, which unlocks 5 of T-Rexy's looks.
     - Jigsaws: Peek and Fix one are used on the first; every jigsaw is solved by clicking tiles; none may have holes.
     - Clue words: the first uses Scan after wrong letters, the second runs out of fuel and is typed to refuel.
     - Clue typing, part styles, paint, songs, the four mystery questions (one wrong answer must show a clue), the shrink, the ending.
     - After the first portal the page is reloaded, and "Keep going" must resume on the crash pad with the clue saved.
     - Right answers move on by themselves; the ship comes alive in the end clip; the high score saves and the secret
       ending shows (all four pages).
Prints PASS or FAIL with the reasons, and exits 1 on FAIL.

files.about: Makes the shareable QR card for a game's newest release in that game's own colors and icons, with the title and version and a QR code that opens the game's permanent home page ("home" in game.json). Starward gets its night sky, gold four-point stars, and rocket; a game can set its own look with a "qr" block in game.json (Mini Game Survival: neon colors, spikes, jigsaw pieces, and T-Rexy's head). Checks that the finished card scans back to the right link.
files.requires: kit/base.css, assets/fx/defs.svg, assets/icons/icons.js, assets/characters/trexy.js (colors and icon shapes are copied from these)
files.notes:
Usage, from the library folder:
  python3 build/qr.py games/starward/game.json     card for the newest release in game.json
Writes dist/<id>-v<N>-qr.png. Needs Pillow and opencv-python-headless (pip install opencv-python-headless).
Uses the qrcode package when installed (pip install "qrcode[pil]"); otherwise OpenCV's own QR encoder makes the code.
Exits 1 if the card does not scan back to the release link.

Optional "qr" block in game.json:
  { "colors": { void, nebula, nebulaHi, starlight, dust, glow, accent, gold, onGold }, "badge": "star" | "trexy", "cta": "Scan to play!" }

files.about: Building blocks for obstacle runs: short stretches of spikes, steps, bounce pads, gaps, ship tunnels, and one secret stretch with a hidden box up high. A run is put together from these, gentle ones at low levels and trickier ones at high levels.
files.provides: Kit.levels.runner (list of chunks)
files.notes:
Format is described in kit/runner.js. min and max are the run levels (1 to 6) a chunk can appear at, w is how often it is picked.
Every chunk starts with at least 2 tiles of flat ground. The hero's hop is tiny (about 1.25 tiles) and his double hop reaches
about 2.3 tiles, so anything 3 tiles high needs a bounce pad. Level 1 only uses things a single hop or a bounce pad clears,
with lots of flat ground between them; the double hop just makes the timing forgiving. The level generator plays each chunk
with its solver before using it, so a chunk that can't be beaten at some speed is simply skipped there.
tag "ship" = a ship tunnel (between a ship portal S and a hero portal C). tag "secret" = holds the hidden box x, reached by
hopping onto a thin ledge with a pad on it; running straight under the ledge is the normal way through.

files.about: 46 fill-in-the-blank sentences about space, robots, and science for ages 8 to 10, each tagged easy (1), medium (2), or hard (3). ___ marks the blank.
files.provides: Kit.questions.banks.blanks

files.about: 21 Earth and geography questions (continents, oceans, mountains, deserts, famous places), each tagged easy (1), medium (2), or hard (3).
files.provides: Kit.questions.banks.earth

files.about: Math question generators that make new problems every time: space word problems, missing numbers, place value, rounding, and number patterns. Each takes a level from 1 to 5. Level 1 is early second grade, 3 is third grade, 5 is fourth grade.
files.provides: Kit.questions.gens { word, missing, place, round, pattern }
files.notes:
Number ranges by level:
  add       1: 1-10        2: 10-60      3: 100-450     4: 150-900     5: 1,000-5,000
  subtract  1: within 20   2: within 100 3: within 1,000 (bigger gaps at 4) 5: within 10,000
  multiply  1: x2, x5, x10 2: up to 5x5  3: up to 9x9   4: 1 digit x 2 digits   5: 2 digits x 2 digits
  divide    matches multiply (always comes out even)

files.about: Generator for "which one does not belong?" puzzles: three things from one group and one sneaky outsider. Level 1 mixes very different groups (tools and planets); level 3 is trickier (the Moon among planets).
files.provides: Kit.questions.gens.odd

files.about: Generator for planet-order questions. Level 1 asks about Earth's neighbors, level 2 about any planet, level 3 asks "which planet is fifth from the Sun?"
files.provides: Kit.questions.gens.order, Kit.questions.PLANETS

files.about: 36 STEM-leaning riddles for ages 8 to 10, each tagged easy (1), medium (2), or hard (3). The clue is what a helper friend says when asked.
files.provides: Kit.questions.banks.riddles

files.about: 48 science and space words to unscramble, from 4 to 7 letters. Longer words are harder, so games choose the length from the player's level.
files.provides: Kit.questions.banks.scramble (each item has len)

files.about: 17 space riddles (planets, stars, comets, rovers), each tagged easy (1), medium (2), or hard (3). Each has two clues: one for a sniff hint and one for a ponder hint.
files.provides: Kit.questions.banks.space

files.about: Science words with kid-friendly hints for word-guessing games, in four topics: sound and music, food and dinosaurs, light and shadows, and space. Each word is tagged easy (1), medium (2), or hard (3).
files.provides: Kit.words.clues { sound, food, light, space } each a list of [WORD, difficulty, hint]
files.notes:
Easy words are 4 or 5 letters, medium 5 to 7, hard 6 to 11. Hints never use the word itself. No word appears in two topics,
so one game never asks the same word twice. About 35 words a topic, so replays keep finding new ones.

files.about: The first game: a tall, scared robot types his way across four planets, solves riddles, and makes friends (a magic puppy, a penguin, and a mossy rock) on the way to the flame that relights his world. Kept as one legacy file; its characters, music style, and question ideas live on in the library as Starward's modules.
Original single-file source, kept unchanged so this version can always be rebuilt or edited.

Starts Mini Game Survival: connects each story step type to its screen, resumes saved games (rebuilding the scene from the story so far), turns on Enter-to-continue, lets L and R (or the arrow keys) step back and forward through the story, skipping mini games already finished, and keeps the game going through live page updates.

Mini Game Survival's neon look: hot pink, laser cyan, and glitch yellow colors on a deep purple night, a glitchy title, the Easy and Hard picker, the wide scene during runs, the jigsaw board over the scene, the clue notebook and secret diary pages, the run buttons, the mystery choices, the part and paint pickers, the keep-going or run-again choice and the bonus line, the hint bubble, and touch-screen extras (tap words, back and forward buttons, the phone keyboard button).

T-Rexy, a cute little T-Rex with a tiny jump, wakes up alone in the glitchy neon Glitch Nebula after weird music swoops him away from home. He runs four obstacle portals (bounce pads, ship tunnels, spikes), rebuilds his memories in jigsaw puzzles, spells science clue words before the glitch drains his fuel, types each clue into his notebook, and builds a spaceship to get home. Then he solves the mystery of Shadowspine, the giant all-black Spinosaurus. Hidden diary pages and other secrets, hardcore music, adaptive difficulty, and an arcade high score board.

Mini Game Survival's question library, so every game is different: eight versions of each mystery question, several ways to tell what T-Rexy saw in each memory, six ways to write each clue line T-Rexy types into his notebook (short, medium, and long), eight ways to say each clue card's key science fact, and fourteen fun bonus facts for each portal. The game deals versions like a shuffled deck kept on this computer, so nothing repeats until every version has come up (see deal and pickVersion in state.js). The clue words themselves live in content/words/clue-words.js.
files.notes:
QBANK.mystery: the four mystery steps, in order. Each has clue (which notebook clue helps), nope (the hint after a wrong answer),
  and v: versions { q, opts, a } where a is the index of the right option. Every version of a step must test the same idea,
  because the reveal depends on all four. Never name Nova here: the player doesn't meet her until after the mystery.
QBANK.saw[portal]: ways to tell what T-Rexy saw in that portal's memory (the top of the clue card). Every version keeps the clue.
QBANK.lines[portal]: three lists (typing level 1, 2, 3) of clue lines to type. Each says the same clue in different words.
QBANK.facts[portal]: ways to say the clue card's key science fact (this fact helps solve the mystery, so every version keeps it).
QBANK.bonus[portal]: fun extra facts, one shown on each clue card.
To add a version, add a row. Keep the reading level for grades 2 to 6, keep every clue true to the story, and keep every fact true.

files.notes:
tip(keys, tap): a hint with a keyboard version and a touch version. showHint and hintIfIdle (scene.js) take one and pick the
  right words when the hint shows. In HTML, put keyboard-only words in a .k-only span and touch-only words in a .t-only span.
phoneKeyboard(host) -> { stop }: adds an "Open keyboard" button to host that opens the phone's keyboard. Each letter typed
  becomes a key press for the typing challenge on screen. Letters from a real keyboard already reach the challenge, so
  they're never sent twice. stop() closes the keyboard.

Adaptive difficulty. Tracks how the player is doing in each skill and moves that skill's level up or down. Levels are remembered on that computer for that game.
files.provides: Kit.adaptive.create({ key, skills, onChange }) -> { level(skill), record(skill, outcome), adjust(skill, delta), snapshot() }
files.notes:
skills: { name: { min, max, start } }, for example { math: { min: 1, max: 5, start: 3 } }
record(skill, outcome) rules:
  "clean"    solved on the first try with no hints. Two in a row: level up.
  "ok"       solved after one miss or with a hint. Level stays the same.
  "struggle" solved after two or more misses. Two in a row: level down.
  "gaveup"   needed "Show me". Level down right away.
adjust(skill, +1 or -1) changes a level directly (typing rounds use this).
onChange(skill, newLevel, delta) runs whenever a level actually changes.

files.notes:
run options:
  arena      element the words fall through (position: absolute; inset: 0)
  panel      element for the typing display
  head       HTML shown at the top of the panel

files.about: Runs a game's story as a list of steps (say a line, show a puzzle, fly, and so on). Each step type has a handler. Also holds the cleanup for whatever screen is showing, so leaving a screen always stops its timers and key listeners.
files.provides: Kit.flow.create({ steps, handlers, beforeStep }) -> { go, next, step, token, alive, bump, setCleanup, cleanupNow, replay }
files.notes:
A handler returns true when its step is instant (change world, add a friend); the flow then moves straight to the next step.
token() and alive(t) let slow actions (countdowns, walks) check they still belong to the current screen.
replay(upto, { type: fn }) re-applies instant steps when resuming a saved game.

files.about: Styles for the letter-guessing game: the hint, the secret word's letter boxes, the fuel tank cells (they flicker when zapped), and the on-screen letter keys.

A friendly letter-guessing game (no hangman): a secret word, a riddle-style hint, and a fuel tank. Type or tap letters to guess. Right letters light up in the word; each wrong letter drains one fuel cell. If the fuel runs out, the word is shown and the player types it to refuel and keep going, so nobody gets stuck.
files.provides: Kit.fuelWord.render(panel, options) -> { use(key) }
files.notes:
options = { head (HTML), tip (one short line), word, hint, fuel (number of cells), cheers, autoNext (ms, default 1700),
            scanAfter (wrong letters before the Scan helper pulses, default 2), helperHtml (icon for the Scan button),
            onGuess(letter, ok), onScan(), onOut(), onWin({ misses, scans, out, fuelLeft, cheer }), onDone() }
use("scan") presses the Scan helper from outside the panel (for example, tapping the hero); it reveals one letter, once.

files.about: A bouncier music player for upbeat, dance-style chiptune songs written as data: sixteenth-note patterns, verse and chorus sections, claps and open hi-hats, sparkly chord arpeggios, an octave-bouncing bass, and a pulse-wave lead with a little echo. Same controls as kit/music.js, so the jukebox works with it, and it plays kit/music.js songs too. Everything is synthesized in code (no audio files, nothing copyrighted).
files.provides: Kit.groove.create(songs) -> { set(id), restart(id, { at, delay }), hush(), position(), unlock(), setEnabled(on), enabled, want }, Kit.groove.render(audioContext, song, seconds)
files.notes:
Song format (see assets/music/glitch-hub.js):
  title, bpm (quarter notes a minute; each step is a sixteenth note), root (MIDI note of the key, 60 = middle C)
  form       section names in play order, looped, for example ["A", "B", "A", "C"]
  sections   { name: { chords, lead, bass, kick, clap, hat, open, arp } }
    chords   one chord per bar, each a list of semitones above root (the first one is the bass note)
    lead     a string of steps, 16 per bar: a number = semitones above root (plus the lead's oct), . = rest, - = keep holding
    bass     a pattern repeated every bar: 1 = chord root, 8 = root an octave up, 5 = the fifth, . = rest, - = hold
    kick, clap, hat, open   patterns: x = hit, . = rest (16 per bar, or longer to cover several bars, for fills)
    arp      true to ripple the chord's notes every sixteenth
  lead, arp, bass, pad   instrument settings: { wave: square | triangle | sawtooth | sine | pulse25 | pulse12, vol, oct, echo, gate }
  drums      { kick, clap, hat, open } volumes
Songs written for kit/music.js (32 eighth-note steps, no form) still play: they are turned into this format.
render(ctx, song, seconds) schedules a song into any audio context from time 0 (the play-test uses it to check loudness).
restart(id, { at, delay }) plays a song from `at` seconds in (a negative `at` waits that long first), starting `delay` seconds
from now and cutting off notes already lined up, so a game can keep the music in time with something (a rhythm run).
hush() fades the music out right away until the next set or restart. position() = seconds into the song now, or null.

files.about: Styles for the picture jigsaw: the tile grid, the selected tile, tiles that are home (locked with a glow), glitchy gaps for missing pieces, the peek overlay, and the solved picture.

Picture jigsaw: a picture is cut into a grid of tiles and shuffled. Swap two tiles to fix it. Works with arrow keys and Enter, or by clicking two tiles. Tiles that are home lock in place with a glow. Helpers can peek at the whole picture or put one tile home. Pieces the player never found can be left out: they stay as glitchy gaps in the finished picture, even when peeking.
files.provides: Kit.jigsaw.render(board, options) -> { peek(), fix(), stop(), placed(), total }

files.about: Styles for the jukebox song list and the "New song!" title.
A list of collected songs with play and stop buttons. Songs not found yet show as locked.
files.provides: Kit.jukebox.render(el, { order, songs, owned, where, music, icons, onTurnOn, fallback })
files.notes:
order     song ids in display order
songs     Kit.songs (each has a title)
owned()   ids the player has collected; the first id in order is always owned
where(id) where the song is found, shown under its title
music     the player made by Kit.music.create
icons     { note, play, stop } HTML
onTurnOn  called if pressing play had to switch music back on
fallback  song id to return to when a playing song is stopped (default: the first in order)

files.about: Plays looping background songs that are written as data and synthesized in code (no audio files, nothing copyrighted).
files.provides: Kit.music.create(songs) -> { set(id), unlock(), setEnabled(on), enabled, want }
files.notes:
Song format (see assets/music/*.js):
  title     name shown in jukeboxes
  bpm       tempo; each step is an eighth note
  root      MIDI note number of the key (60 = middle C)
  lead      32 steps: semitones above root, or null for a rest
  chords    4 chords (one per 8 steps), each a list of semitone offsets
  bass      8 steps: 1 = chord root, 2 = root an octave up, 0 = rest
  kick, hat 8 steps of 1 or 0 (optional drums)
  optional: wave, oct, pluck, leadVol, leadLen, pad, padWave, bassWave, bassVol, bassLen, hatVol

files.about: Styles for the puzzle screen: question kind tag, fill-in blank, letter tiles, helper buttons, clues, and right or wrong feedback (a big popping cheer for a right answer).
Shows one question with an answer box, helper buttons, and feedback. Works with every question kind in kit/questions.js (riddles, fill in the blank, scrambles, number patterns, odd one out, math).
files.provides: Kit.puzzleUI { render(panel, question, options) -> { use(helperKey) }, blankHTML }
files.notes:
options:
  head        HTML above the question (place name, progress dots)
  leave       function for a "walk away" back button (optional)
  helpers     [{ key, type: "scan" | "clue" | "peek" | "clue2", label, iconHtml, color, who, onUse }] in display order
              scan = show how many letters; clue = show question.clue; peek = reveal a letter; clue2 = show question.clue2
  icons       { check, eye, back } HTML
  autoNext    ms to show the cheer after a right answer before moving on by itself (default 1700; a shown spelling or answer adds 900).
              0 shows a Next button instead.
  nextHtml    HTML for that Next button (only used when autoNext is 0)
  cheers      cheers to pick from after a right answer (default: a few general ones)
  showAfter   wrong answers before "Show me" appears (default 3)
  onHint(type), onWrong(tries), onNudge(helperKey), onWin({ shown, tries, hints, spell, cheer }), onDone()

render returns { use(key) }: presses a helper from outside the panel (for example, tapping a friend
on the stage). It returns true if the helper was used, false if it is used up, hidden, or the puzzle is gone.

files.about: The question system: banks of written questions, generators that make new ones on the fly, a picker that matches the player's level and avoids repeats across games, and the answer checker.
files.provides: Kit.questions { addBank, banks, gens, KIND, createPicker, judge, scrambled }

files.about: Side-scrolling obstacle run, like a rhythm platformer: the hero runs by himself, hops over spikes (and hops again in the air for a double hop), bounces off pads, and flies a little ship through tunnels. Touching a spike or a wall sends him back to the start (or the last checkpoint, once checkpoints are on). Levels are built from chunks with flat ground between them for breathing room, and a built-in solver plays every chunk before it is used, so every level can be beaten. Given the music's tempo, each chunk's first hop lands on a beat, the ground and pads pulse with the beat, and a hop right on the beat over danger pops a "PERFECT!". Catching a piece bursts into sparkles, landings puff a little dust, and crashes give the screen a small shake.
files.provides: Kit.runner { sim: { DT, PHYS, Level, start, step, clone, solve, checkPieces }, generate(options), play(canvas, options) -> { stop, pause(on), checkpoints(on), skip(), state } }
files.notes:
Units are tiles and seconds. The ground's top is y = 0, and y goes up. The physics runs in fixed 1/120 s steps,
so a list of button presses (one per step) always replays exactly the same way.
Hopping: hold the button on the ground to hop (keep holding to hop again on landing). Press again in the air for one double hop.
Running off a ledge still allows a normal hop for a few steps (coyote time). A quick tap always counts, even between frames.

Chunk format (see content/levels/runner-chunks.js): { id, min, max, len, w, tag, gaps: [[x0, x1]], o: [[kind, x, y, w, h]] }
  kinds: b block (x, y, w, h), s spike pointing up (x, y), v spike hanging down (x, y = its top), p bounce pad (x, y),
         S ship portal (x), C hero portal (x), x secret box (x, y). Ground is added under the chunk except in gaps.

generate({ chunks, level, speed, length, pieces, rng, secret, ships, space, beat }) -> { L, inputs, checks, endX, secret: { from, inputs } | null, frames, spans, beat }
  Picks chunks for the level, proves each one can be beaten, then places memory pieces along the winning path.
  ships = how many ship tunnels to try for (0 = none), space = extra tiles of flat ground before each chunk.
  Pass a seeded rng to get the same level again (for a second try at the same run).
  Pieces only go where the hero runs along the ground on the winning path: never in mid-air, never in a ship tunnel,
  never in the secret stretch (so the secret route gets them all too), and never touching a block, spike, pad, or portal.
  spans = [{ id, tag, x0, x1 }] where each chunk sits (games use it for hints about what the player crashed on).
  beat = seconds per beat of the run's music (0 = off). Each chunk is nudged forward so the spot where the hero should hop
  (or hit a pad, or reach a ship portal) for its first obstacle comes exactly on a beat, counting from the run's start.
  The result's beat = { tiles (tiles per beat), actions: [hero x at each chunk's first hop] } (the play-test checks it).
sim.checkPieces(gen) -> list of problems (empty when every piece can be caught on the normal and secret routes).

play(canvas, { gen, theme, label, have, beat, drawBackground(ctx, view), drawHero(ctx, x, y, size, hero), onCrash(n, info),
              onCollect(obj), onMode(mode), onDouble(), onPerfect(streak), onClock(seconds, running), onFinish(result),
              autopilot(), speedup(), drop(), tip, pauseTip })
  beat = seconds per beat (same as generate's): the ground, pads, and pieces pulse on it, and a hop pressed within about
  0.09 s of a beat that carries the hero over a spike, gap, or step pops "PERFECT!" when he lands (onPerfect(streak);
  a streak counts perfect hops in a row and a crash resets it).
  onClock(seconds, running) tells a game when the run's clock starts or jumps (start, respawn, unpause: running = true,
  seconds = where the run is now) or stops (crash, pause, finish: running = false), so it can keep the music in time.
  have = indices of pieces already found on an earlier try: they count from the start and show as faint outlines.
  The screen shows no attempt counter. onCrash(n, info) gets a running count for this run only (so a game can offer
  help) and info = { x, why, mode, chunk: { id, tag } | null, pressed (has the player pressed jump yet) }; nothing is
  kept after the run. result = { crashes, pieces, piecesTotal, gotIdx, secret, usedCheckpoints, skipped, perfects, ms }
  drop() is a play-test hook: that many of the first pieces can't be caught.
  tip = words shown near the top for the first few seconds (shrunk to fit a narrow screen). pauseTip = the line under
  PAUSED (default "Space to keep going"). Hop with Space, Up, W, a click, or a tap. Tiles are about a ninth of the
  screen's height, but at least 15 tiles fit across, so a narrow screen (like a phone) still shows what's coming.
  hero (for drawHero) = { mode, vy, grounded, h, t, spin } where spin goes 0 to 1 during a double hop's flip, else -1.

files.provides: Kit.starfield.create(canvas, { color, count }) -> { boost(), warp(on), pause(on) }

files.about: A walkable top-down map on a canvas. The player moves with arrow keys, WASD, or by clicking; walking into a place triggers it. Includes fog with light holes, particle bursts, speech bubbles, and an arrow-key hint until the player first moves.
files.provides: Kit.topdownMap.create(options) -> map { start(pos), stop(), on, busy, pos, say(text, ms), burst(x, y, color, n), stepOutOf(site) }
files.notes:
options:
  canvas, width, height       map size in map units (the canvas scales to fit)
  speed, enterRadius          walking speed (units per second) and how close counts as "arrived"
  bounds                      { minX, maxX, minY, maxY } where the player can walk
  sites                       [{ id, x, y }] places that trigger onArrive
  drawWorld(c, t)             draw ground and places (map units)
  drawPlayer(c, x, y, t, m)   draw the player; m = { moving, phase, fx, fy }
  drawAbove(c, t)             draw things that sit above the fog (beacons)
  fog                         { rgb: "r,g,b", alpha(), holes(pos) -> [{ x, y, r, a }] } (optional)
  onArrive(site), onMove(), showHint() -> boolean
  colors                      { light, dark } for bubbles and the arrow-key hint
  font                        font family for speech bubbles

files.about: Two untimed typing challenges. dig: type the words written on clumps of dirt to dig something up. line: type one sentence exactly (like a brave promise).
files.provides: Kit.typing { dig(panel, options) -> stop, line(panel, options) -> stop }

files.about: Styles for typing challenges: falling word chips, the countdown, the big word display, the accuracy goal bar, the caught-star row, and the dirt clumps for digging.
Shared screen helpers: the main Next button, progress dots, toasts, focus, Enter-to-continue, and reading theme colors for canvas drawing.
files.provides: Kit.ui { reduced, focusSoon, bindPrimary, nextBtn, pips, toaster, enterAdvances, tokens, blurActive }

files.about: Small helpers every game uses: finding elements, random picks, answer matching, and safe browser storage.
files.provides: Kit.util { $, wait, shuffle, sample, pick, rint, clamp, esc, norm, squash, lev, cleanName, store }

files.about: Cartoon voices. For villains: an evil laugh and a grumbly mutter for when a villain talks. The laugh is a real recording when the game includes recorded laughs (like assets/sounds/villain-laughs.js), taking turns between them; otherwise it's made in code, like the mutter: each syllable a buzzy tone shaped by vowel filters, with a breathy "h" or a humming "m" at the start, plus a little echo. For cute characters: chirp plays a real recorded happy creature noise (like assets/sounds/dino-chirps.js), pitched up or down so each character sounds like itself.
files.provides: Kit.voices { evilLaugh(options) -> seconds, mutter(seconds, options) -> seconds, chirp(options) -> seconds, clipBuffer(audioContext, clip) -> Promise<AudioBuffer | null> }
files.notes:
evilLaugh({ clip (which recorded laugh, default: take turns), volume (0 to 1, default .85), synth (true = the made-in-code laugh),
            pitch (Hz, default 120), has (how many HAs, default 4), squeak (true to end with a tiny voice crack; default: now and then) })
  Recorded laughs come from Kit.sounds.villainLaughs: [{ id, seconds, src (data: URL) }]. A new laugh cuts off the one still playing.
mutter(seconds, { pitch })
chirp({ mood (happy | excited | curious, default happy), pitch (1 = as recorded, 2 = an octave higher, .8 = lower; default 1),
        volume (0 to 1, default .7), clip (an id, to pick one), at (seconds from now, default 0) })
  Plays one recorded noise from Kit.sounds.dinoChirps: [{ id, mood, seconds, src (data: URL) }], never the same one twice in a row
  when there's a choice. Pitch also changes speed, like a record player, so a bigger character gets a lower, slower voice.
  Returns 0 when the game has no recorded noises.
All three return how long they last, so a game can animate along with them. They stay silent when sound is off (Kit.audio.setEnabled),
but still return their length. Pass { ctx: someAudioContext, at: seconds } to draw into another context (the play-test uses this).

games.title: The Inner Flame
games.about: The first game: a tall, scared robot types his way across four planets, solves riddles, and makes friends (a magic puppy, a penguin, and a mossy rock) on the way to the flame that relights his world. Kept as one legacy file; its characters, music style, and question ideas live on in the library as Starward's modules.

releases.notes: Original game, designed by Child I by voice.

games.title: Mini Game Survival v6
games.about: T-Rexy, a cute little T-Rex with a tiny jump, wakes up alone in the glitchy neon Glitch Nebula after weird music swoops him away from home. He runs four obstacle portals (bounce pads, ship tunnels, spikes), rebuilds his memories in jigsaw puzzles, spells science clue words before the glitch drains his fuel, types each clue into his notebook, and builds a spaceship to get home. Then he solves the mystery of Shadowspine, the giant all-black Spinosaurus. Hidden diary pages and other secrets, hardcore music, adaptive difficulty, and an arcade high score board.

releases.notes: First version: four portals (obstacle runs, memory jigsaws, glitch-locked clue words, clue typing), the Shadow Gate, the mystery of Shadowspine, secret diary pages, hardcore songs, adaptive levels, high scores.

Easier runs that ramp up portal by portal, a double hop, Easy and Hard modes, no attempt counting, a funnier opening with dinosaur and space puns, upbeat music, NASA-inspired neon backgrounds, detailed memory pictures, a one-piece Shadowspine with an evil laugh, a question library, and the Zoomasaurus end clip.

Every memory piece catchable (checked in every play-test), missing pieces leave holes in the memory jigsaw with a keep-going or run-again choice and a full-catch bonus, L and R move back and forward through the story, hints that show the keys only when a player is stuck, and a real recorded villain laugh (CC0).

Checkpoints always on; Hard mode needs every memory piece to move on; obstacles on the beat with the music kept in time; PERFECT hops; catch sparkles, landing dust, and a crash shake; 12 unlockable looks for T-Rexy and his closet on the crash pad.

A cuter, more expressive T-Rexy: big shiny eyes, a brow that shows his mood, rosier blush, new faces (blink, excited, determined, worried with a sweat drop), blinking, reactions during runs, and squash and stretch on hops.

games.title: Starward v6
games.about: A tall robot, the Keeper of Lumina, explores his dark home world to rebuild his rocket, then flies to four planets with new friends to bring back the Everlight. Typing flights, STEM puzzles, collectible songs, adaptive difficulty, and an arcade high score board.

releases.notes: First Starward: new names and story, rocket parts on Lumina, falling-word flights, fill-in-the-blank puzzles, songs, high scores. Kept in that page's version history (version 1 of the page).
Walkable Lumina map, three challenges per rocket part, fresh questions every game, fewer instructions. Current version of that page. Single-file source: games/starward/legacy/v3.html
Rebuilt from the library. Adaptive difficulty for typing, math, and word puzzles; questions chosen to match the player's level.

Same game as v4 with no personal names: the title screen says "An original space adventure". The first version on the permanent home page, whose high scores now carry across updates. Archived to its own page on 2026-10-17 when v6 shipped.

One-line tip on every Lumina dig; a big cheer after a right answer, then the game moves on by itself (no Next button); safe landings and the brave words move on by themselves; tap Sunny on the stage or in the friends bar to sniff for a clue (Rigel peeks, Professor Kepler ponders).
